newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain strike punch dulled, govt said unruffled.
newsitem.headline: Spain strike punch dulled, govt said unruffled.

text.p: Striking Spanish truckers' grip on the nation appeared to be diminishing on Tuesday as the government guaranteed the security of traffic and provided escorts through picketed areas where requested.
Trade unions accused the administration of being in no hurry to resolve the 13-day old dispute, which hinges on truckers' demands for earlier retirement and lower fuel costs.
Jose Luis Soldevilla, head of the strike committee at truckers' union Fedatrans said talks were blocked.
"The government is in no hurry to negotiate because it thinks the situation is righting itself, or is tending towards normalisation," he told local press late on Monday.
The government denied this was the case, saying the administration had been willing to resolve the conflict from the outset. Moreover, talks were making progress.

"We've had something of an approximation of views in some respects, and (the union is) exaggerating the implications of the talks so far. They know if we gave in to their demands it would mean the bankruptcy of the social security system," a Development Ministry spokesman told Reuters.
The main bone of contention is the strikers' demands for retirement at 60 instead of 65, maintaining pension allowances.
While negotiations continued, the Spanish government was guaranteeing free traffic movement nationwide.
"The transport situation is completely normal, traffic is flowing freely and the civil guard continues to guarantee free circulation," a source at the Interior Ministry said.
"Today there were some lorry escorts, but there's really been no incidents, apart from some broken windows," she added.
A government official in the northern region of Cantabria warned this morning that hoarding fuel and food supplies was not only illegal but unnecessary, national radio reported.
The region was guaranteeing police escorts for transporters who feared reprisals from truckers lined along major roads, and provided a helpline number.
In the central south-eastern region on Monday local police detained 19 pickets after they forced a lorry to stop and two of the pickets attacked the driver, who was slightly injured.
But the Interior Ministry said there was no area that was gravely damaged by the stoppage, including the northern region which was severely impacted last week.
"There's no (geographical) area in particular that's been affected, and everything is going on normally," a source said.
Carmakers have been forced to cut back or halt production for lack of parts, but most effects of the effects on the economy are left over from last week's bigger-scale disruptions.
While the government insisted that it was business as usual, carmaker stoppages prompted fears that foreigners might take their business elsewhere.
But corporate officials seemed unruffled.
A General Motors official said the U.S. auto giant, which produces the Opel and Vauxhall brands in Europe, was not contemplating changing its supplier contracts in Spain.
"There's always the possiblity of some workstoppage in any European country. There can be a strike anywhere. Those kind of things are part and parcel of democratic processes," he said.
Volkswagen said it expected virtually no long-term sales loss from the Spanish strike.
Some French and British trucks are stranded in the north.

Around 100 British drivers are still stuck in the Basque region. Although there were worries for their personal safety, police escorts seemed to be allaying fears elsewhere, the UK Freight Transport Association said.
